_provenance.what: Details-panel knowledge for the United States wine map, US-4: the 42 AVAs of Washington, Oregon and New York (spec docs/superpowers/specs/2026-09-29-usa-wine-map-design.md §10; plan docs/superpowers/plans/2026-09-30-usa-wine-map-us4.md). Turned into supabase/migrations/20260930234747_usa_us4_knowledge.sql by scripts/wine-map-sources/gen-place-profiles-migration.mjs --source data/wine-map/place-profiles-usa-us4.json --bare.
_provenance.written_in_session: From 2026-09-30, from public sources only (listed under each place); no API batch (AGENTS.md).
_provenance.rules: Plain English, no praise words, figures only where a listed source publishes them, never 'official boundary' (spec §18). Exactly one key fact 'Established YYYY (27 CFR 9.N)', as TTB lists it. Descriptions of 2-4 sentences, at most 700 characters. At most 8 grapes; the 1-3 signature grapes are PRINCIPAL and the rest ACCESSORY. At least two sources per place, one of them the CFR section or the Federal Register final rule. share_pct is left out. New grapes only from the US-4 allow-list (hybrids; never a labrusca), each with a source.

article.description: An AVA about 60 miles east of Portland that lies on both banks of the Columbia River, in Oregon and Washington: Hood River and Wasco counties, Oregon, and Skamania and Klickitat counties, Washington. The river cuts the only sea-level passage through the Cascade Range, and over a short distance the climate shifts from wet and marine-influenced in the west to dry high desert in the east.
article.climate: Rainfall drops from about 36 inches a year near the Cascades to about 10 inches in the east, and winds funnelled through the gorge, often 10 to 20 mph or more, cool and dry the vineyards. Vineyards range from near sea level to about 2,000 feet.
article.soils: Volcanic soils, lahar deposits, loess, silt and sand; the final rule names silty loams of the Chemawa, Underwood and McGowen series, on benchlands left by ancient lava flows.
article.grape_varieties: Many varieties: Pinot Noir, Chardonnay, Gewürztraminer and Riesling in the cooler, wetter west, and Zinfandel and Cabernet Sauvignon in the drier east.
article.wine_styles: White wines from Chardonnay, Gewürztraminer and Riesling, and red wines from Pinot Noir in the west and from Zinfandel and Cabernet Sauvignon in the east.
key_facts: Hood River and Wasco counties (Oregon); Skamania and Klickitat counties (Washington)
About 186,610 acres, 120,010 of them in Oregon (Oregon Wine Board)

sources.title: 27 CFR 9.178, Columbia Gorge (eCFR text via Cornell LII)
Federal Register final rule (govinfo), T.D. TTB-11, Columbia Gorge (2004)
Oregon Wine Board, Columbia Gorge AVA
Great Northwest Wine (Kitsap Daily News), on the Columbia Gorge (2014)

article.description: A large AVA in Jackson and Josephine counties, within the Southern Oregon AVA, made up of three distinct valleys with progressively warmer climates along the Rogue River and its tributaries. It lies about 75 miles from the coast, framed by the Cascade, Siskiyou and Coast ranges. Peter Britt began growing grapes here around 1852 and in 1873 founded Valley View, Oregon's first official winery.
article.climate: Warm, dry summers, with nights much cooler than the days, which keeps acidity in the grapes and lengthens the ripening season.
article.soils: Mainly stream sediments laid down by the Rogue River and its tributaries, varying from one of its three valleys to the next.
article.grape_varieties: Cabernet Sauvignon, Syrah and Viognier lead, with Pinot Noir, Chardonnay and Pinot Gris.
article.wine_styles: Red wines from Cabernet Sauvignon, Syrah and Pinot Noir, and white wines from Viognier, Chardonnay and Pinot Gris.

sources.title: 27 CFR 9.132, Rogue Valley (eCFR text via Cornell LII)
Oregon Wine Board, Rogue Valley AVA

article.description: An AVA in the Siskiyou Mountains of Jackson and Josephine counties, entirely within the Rogue Valley AVA, running about 50 miles north from the California border to the Rogue River near Grants Pass. The surrounding ranges shelter it from cool Pacific winds. Most vineyards lie on stream terraces and alluvial fans shaped by the Applegate River.
article.climate: Hot days and cool nights, with vineyards at up to about 2,000 feet, sheltered from marine air by the mountains around it.
article.soils: Deep, well-drained stream sediments on terraces and alluvial fans laid down by the Applegate River.
article.grape_varieties: Merlot, Cabernet Sauvignon and Syrah lead, with Chardonnay, Tempranillo and Pinot Noir.
article.wine_styles: Full-bodied red wines in Bordeaux and Rhône styles from Merlot, Cabernet Sauvignon and Syrah, and white wine from Chardonnay.
key_facts: About 278,190 acres, about 750 planted (Oregon Wine Board)
Modern winemaking here resumed in the 1970s

sources.title: 27 CFR 9.165, Applegate Valley (eCFR text via Cornell LII)
Oregon Wine Board, Applegate Valley AVA

article.description: An AVA entirely within Douglas County in southwest Oregon, within the Southern Oregon AVA, known for the 'hundred valleys' formed where three mountain ranges meet. German immigrants grew grapes here from the 1880s, and in 1961 Richard Sommer founded HillCrest Vineyard, where he planted Oregon's first Pinot Noir vines. It contains the Elkton Oregon and Red Hill Douglas County, Oregon AVAs.
article.climate: Three broad zones: the cool, marine-influenced north around Elkton, with about 50 inches of rain a year; a central zone near Roseburg that suits both cool- and warm-climate grapes; and a warmer, drier south.
article.soils: Stream sediments, marine sedimentary bedrock and volcanic soils, changing from one small valley to the next.
article.grape_varieties: Pinot Noir and Pinot Gris lead, with Syrah, Tempranillo, Merlot and Albariño.
article.wine_styles: Red wines from Pinot Noir, Syrah, Tempranillo and Merlot, and white wines from Pinot Gris and Albariño.
key_facts: HillCrest Vineyard, founded by Richard Sommer in 1961

sources.title: 27 CFR 9.89, Umpqua Valley (eCFR text via Cornell LII)
Oregon Wine Board, Umpqua Valley AVA

article.description: An AVA of about 74,900 acres in Douglas County, 33 miles inland from the Pacific along the Umpqua River, within the larger Umpqua Valley AVA. It is the coolest and wettest part of the Umpqua Valley, planted to cool-climate grapes.
article.climate: Marine-influenced, with about 50 inches of rain a year, and cooling breezes along the Umpqua River through the growing season.
article.soils: Residual clay, silt loam, alluvial deposits and river terraces, which hold moisture well and reduce the need to irrigate.
article.grape_varieties: Pinot Noir leads, with Pinot Gris, Gewürztraminer and Riesling.
article.wine_styles: Red wine from Pinot Noir and white wines from Pinot Gris, Gewürztraminer and Riesling.
key_facts: 'Elkton Oregon' and 'Elkton OR' are both terms of viticultural significance

sources.title: 27 CFR 9.229, Elkton Oregon (eCFR text via Cornell LII)
Oregon Wine Board, Elkton Oregon AVA

article.description: A small AVA of about 5,600 acres around a single hill east of Interstate 5 near Rice Hill, between Yoncalla and Oakland in Douglas County, within the Umpqua Valley AVA. The Applegate and Scott pioneer families settled at its base in the mid-1800s, and Jesse Applegate planted Douglas County's first vineyard nearby, in Yoncalla, in 1876.
article.climate: Vineyards at 800 to 1,200 feet, without the shelter of the Coast Range, grow cooler than most of Southern Oregon.
article.soils: Iron-rich, red volcanic Jory soils formed from uplifted ancient basalt.
article.grape_varieties: Pinot Noir and Pinot Gris are the predominant grapes.
article.wine_styles: Red wine from Pinot Noir, leaner and more structured than elsewhere in Southern Oregon, and white wine from Pinot Gris.
key_facts: Its boundary follows the 800-foot contour line (27 CFR 9.190)

sources.title: 27 CFR 9.190, Red Hill Douglas County, Oregon (eCFR text via Cornell LII)
Oregon Wine Board, Red Hill Douglas County AVA

article.description: An AVA of about 3,770 acres near Milton-Freewater in Umatilla County, wholly in Oregon. It lies within the Walla Walla Valley AVA, which in turn lies within the Columbia Valley AVA, on a gently sloping alluvial fan of the Walla Walla River covered in basalt cobbles. Italian immigrants grew grapes here from the 1860s, and modern planting began in the 1990s.
article.climate: Sunny summers with wide swings between day and night and occasional days over 100 °F, at elevations of about 800 to 1,000 feet.
article.soils: About 96% Freewater series soils, very cobbly loam and gravelly silt loam full of loose basalt gravel, cobbles and boulders; the stones encourage deep roots and radiate heat to the grapes.
article.grape_varieties: Syrah leads, with Cabernet Sauvignon and Grenache.
article.wine_styles: Red wines, chiefly Syrah, with Cabernet Sauvignon and Grenache.
key_facts: 'The Rocks of Milton-Freewater' is also a term of viticultural significance

sources.title: 27 CFR 9.249, The Rocks District of Milton-Freewater (eCFR text via Cornell LII)
Federal Register final rule (govinfo), T.D. TTB-127, The Rocks District of Milton-Freewater (2015)
Oregon Wine Board, The Rocks District of Milton-Freewater AVA

article.description: An AVA of about 62,500 acres 19 miles southwest of Portland, in Clackamas, Washington and Yamhill counties, within the Willamette Valley AVA. The Chehalem Mountains are a single landmass of hilltops, ridges and spurs rising to 1,633 feet at Bald Peak. Dick Erath planted its first vineyard in 1968; it contains the Ribbon Ridge and Laurelwood District AVAs.
article.climate: Cool, with the mountains sheltering many vineyards from Columbia Gorge winds; most vineyards lie between 200 and 1,000 feet.
article.soils: Three main soil types: volcanic basalt, marine sediment, and wind-blown loess of the Laurelwood series.
article.grape_varieties: Pinot Noir leads, with Chardonnay, Pinot Gris, Riesling, Pinot Blanc and Gamay.
article.wine_styles: Red wines from Pinot Noir and Gamay, and white wines from Chardonnay, Pinot Gris, Riesling and Pinot Blanc.

sources.title: 27 CFR 9.205, Chehalem Mountains (eCFR text via Cornell LII)
Oregon Wine Board, Chehalem Mountains AVA

article.description: An AVA of about 33,600 acres on the north- and east-facing slopes of the Chehalem Mountains, in Washington and Yamhill counties, entirely within the Chehalem Mountains and Willamette Valley AVAs. It is defined by the near-uniform presence of Laurelwood soil, and it includes the highest point in the Willamette Valley, 1,633 feet.
article.climate: Much like the rest of the northern Willamette Valley, with vineyards between 200 and 1,000 feet on hilly to mountainous ground.
article.soils: Laurelwood soil throughout: a base of basalt about 15 million years old topped by wind-blown silt (loess) laid down over the last 200,000 years, up to about 4 feet deep depending on elevation.
article.grape_varieties: Pinot Noir leads, with Pinot Gris and Chardonnay.
article.wine_styles: Red wine from Pinot Noir and white wines from Pinot Gris and Chardonnay.
key_facts: About 70 vineyards on about 975 acres, and 25 wineries (T.D. TTB-160)
Its boundary follows the 200-, 240- and 250-foot elevation contours in places (27 CFR 9.269)

sources.title: 27 CFR 9.269, Laurelwood District (eCFR text via Cornell LII)
Federal Register final rule (govinfo), T.D. TTB-160, Tualatin Hills and Laurelwood District (2020)
Willamette Valley Wineries Association, Laurelwood District AVA overview

article.description: An AVA of about 3,500 acres on a ridge in northern Yamhill County, northwest of Dundee, within the Chehalem Mountains AVA. The ridge stands above the Chehalem Valley floor like an island. Harry Peterson-Nedry planted Ridgecrest Vineyards here in 1980.
article.climate: The ridge's island-like position shelters it from weather extremes: it warms earlier in the day, cools less at night and escapes the sharpest midsummer heat, giving a long, cool growing season.
article.soils: Marine sediments of the Willakenzie series, younger, finer and more uniform than the sedimentary and volcanic soils around the ridge; well drained and moderately deep.
article.grape_varieties: Pinot Noir leads, with Chardonnay, Pinot Gris, Riesling and Gamay.
article.wine_styles: Red wines from Pinot Noir and Gamay, and white wines from Chardonnay, Pinot Gris and Riesling.
key_facts: Commercial grape growing began in 1982 and winemaking in 1985

sources.title: 27 CFR 9.182, Ribbon Ridge (eCFR text via Cornell LII)
Oregon Wine Board, Ribbon Ridge AVA

article.description: An AVA of hills near Newberg in Yamhill County, entirely within the Willamette Valley AVA; its boundary follows the 200-foot contour line where the hills rise from the flat valley floor. Oregon's wine pioneers planted here from 1965, among them David Lett, Dick Erath, the Knudsens and the Sokol Blossers.
article.climate: Warmer nights and less low-lying fog and frost than the valleys beside it, sheltered by the Chehalem Mountains to the north and the Coast Range to the west. Peaks pass 700 feet and reach 1,067 feet.
article.soils: About 80% Jory series soils: reddish silt, clay and loam weathered from Columbia River basalt, moderately fertile and well drained.
article.grape_varieties: Pinot Noir leads, with Chardonnay, Pinot Gris and Pinot Blanc.
article.wine_styles: Red wine from Pinot Noir, white wines from Chardonnay, Pinot Gris and Pinot Blanc, and sparkling wines.
key_facts: Proposed as 'Red Hills', then renamed to avoid confusion with other areas (T.D. TTB-18)

sources.title: 27 CFR 9.180, Dundee Hills (eCFR text via Cornell LII)
Federal Register final rule (govinfo), T.D. TTB-18, Dundee Hills (2004)
Oregon Wine Board, Dundee Hills AVA

article.description: An AVA northwest of Salem in Polk and Yamhill counties, entirely within the Willamette Valley AVA. Its main ridge, the Eola Hills, runs north to south with lateral ridges running east to west. It lies directly east of the Van Duzer Corridor, a break in the Coast Range that lets cool Pacific air through.
article.climate: Cool ocean air through the Van Duzer Corridor lowers late-summer afternoon temperatures sharply, helping grapes keep their acidity; vineyards lie mostly between 250 and 700 feet.
article.soils: Volcanic basalt from ancient lava flows, with marine sedimentary rocks or alluvial deposits, giving shallow, rocky, well-drained soils.
article.grape_varieties: Pinot Noir leads by far, with Chardonnay, Pinot Gris, Riesling and Gamay.
article.wine_styles: Red wines from Pinot Noir and Gamay, and white wines from Chardonnay, Pinot Gris and Riesling.
key_facts: About 39,200 acres, about 3,040 planted (Oregon Wine Board)
Pinot Noir is about 80% of plantings (Willamette Valley Wineries Association)

sources.title: 27 CFR 9.202, Eola-Amity Hills (eCFR text via Cornell LII)
Oregon Wine Board, Eola-Amity Hills AVA
Willamette Valley Wineries Association, Eola-Amity Hills AVA overview

article.description: An AVA of about 25,000 acres between Corvallis and Eugene in Benton and Lane counties, on the west side of the Lower Long Tom River watershed, within the Willamette Valley AVA. Its vineyards sit on stream-cut ridges running east to west.
article.climate: A rain shadow cast by the Coast Range to the west reduces rainfall, and together with the prevailing winds keeps disease pressure low through the growing season.
article.soils: Shallow Bellpine clay loams formed from uplifted ancient marine sediments, mainly sandstone, which vine roots must penetrate to reach water and nutrients.
article.grape_varieties: Pinot Noir predominates, with Chardonnay, Riesling, Pinot Gris and Sauvignon Blanc.
article.wine_styles: Red wine from Pinot Noir and white wines from Chardonnay, Riesling, Pinot Gris and Sauvignon Blanc.
key_facts: About 575 acres planted, 24 vineyards and 12 wineries (Willamette Valley Wineries Association)
Its boundary uses the 360-, 800- and 1,000-foot elevation contours (27 CFR 9.281)

sources.title: 27 CFR 9.281, Lower Long Tom (eCFR text via Cornell LII)
Willamette Valley Wineries Association, Lower Long Tom AVA overview

article.description: An AVA of about 39,045 acres due west of the town of McMinnville in Yamhill County, entirely within the Willamette Valley AVA, on the east and southeast slopes of the Coast Range foothills. It extends about 20 miles south-southwest toward the Van Duzer Corridor.
article.climate: In the weather shadow of the Coast Range, with less rain than sites further east, and drying winds through the Van Duzer Corridor.
article.soils: Uplifted marine sedimentary loams and silts with alluvial overlays on a basalt base, shallow for grape growing.
article.grape_varieties: Pinot Noir makes up about 84% of plantings, with Chardonnay and Pinot Blanc.
article.wine_styles: Mostly red wine from Pinot Noir, with white wines from Chardonnay and Pinot Blanc.
key_facts: Vineyards between 200 and 1,000 feet (Willamette Valley Wineries Association)
About 750 acres planted in 16 vineyards (Willamette Valley Wineries Association)

sources.title: 27 CFR 9.181, McMinnville (eCFR text via Cornell LII)
Willamette Valley Wineries Association, McMinnville AVA overview

article.description: An AVA of about 5,850 acres around a single mountain in Polk County, within the Willamette Valley AVA, rising from 260 feet at its base to 835 feet at the peak. 'Polk County, Oregon' is part of the name because at least three other places in Oregon are called Mount Pisgah.
article.climate: Cooler than the land nearby, averaging about 2,543 growing degree days against 2,903 at Salem, and much less windy, at an average of 2.3 mph against 6.1 mph at Salem.
article.soils: Ancient sedimentary soils rather than the younger alluvium around the mountain: silty clay loams of the Bellpine, Jory, Nekia, Rickreall and Willakenzie series cover about 92% of the area.
article.grape_varieties: Pinot Noir, Pinot Gris and Chardonnay are the most commonly grown grapes.
article.wine_styles: Red wine from Pinot Noir and white wines from Pinot Gris and Chardonnay.
key_facts: 10 commercial vineyards on about 531 acres, and 2 wineries (T.D. TTB-180)
'Mt. Pisgah, Polk County, Oregon' is also a term of viticultural significance

sources.title: 27 CFR 9.284, Mount Pisgah, Polk County, Oregon (eCFR text via Cornell LII)
Federal Register final rule (govinfo), T.D. TTB-180, Mount Pisgah, Polk County, Oregon (2022)

article.description: An AVA of about 144,000 acres in the northwest corner of the Willamette Valley, in Multnomah and Washington counties, entirely within the Willamette Valley AVA, named for and largely defined by the watershed of the Tualatin River. It is sheltered by the Coast Range to the west and the Chehalem Mountains to the south.
article.climate: A rain shadow gives cooler springs and drier autumns at harvest, with wider day-night swings than the areas around it; vineyards lie between 200 and 1,000 feet.
article.soils: The largest concentration in Oregon of Laurelwood soil, fine, stone-free silt of wind-blown loess and weathered basalt, with the related Kinton and Cornelius series.
article.grape_varieties: Pinot Noir leads, with Pinot Gris, Chardonnay and Gewürztraminer.
article.wine_styles: Red wine from Pinot Noir and white wines from Pinot Gris, Chardonnay and Gewürztraminer.
key_facts: About 1,009 acres planted in 41 vineyards (Willamette Valley Wineries Association)
Average annual rainfall of about 43.7 inches (T.D. TTB-160)

sources.title: 27 CFR 9.268, Tualatin Hills (eCFR text via Cornell LII)
Federal Register final rule (govinfo), T.D. TTB-160, Tualatin Hills and Laurelwood District (2020)
Willamette Valley Wineries Association, Tualatin Hills AVA overview

article.description: An AVA of about 59,850 acres in Polk and Yamhill counties, within the Willamette Valley AVA, at the eastern end of a low wind gap in the Coast Range through which Pacific air flows into the valley. Its low, gently rolling hills widen from the narrow western gap toward the east.
article.climate: Steady, strong winds from the ocean, arriving as early as 2 p.m., cool the vineyards; the wind thickens grape skins and reduces fungal pressure, and heat accumulation stays low.
article.soils: Shallow, well-drained uplifted marine sedimentary loams and silts with alluvial overlay and some uplifted basalt, high in silt and clay, unlike the volcanic and loess soils around it.
article.grape_varieties: Pinot Noir leads, with Chardonnay, Pinot Gris, Riesling, Pinot Blanc and Sauvignon Blanc.
article.wine_styles: Red wine from Pinot Noir and white wines from Chardonnay, Pinot Gris, Riesling, Pinot Blanc and Sauvignon Blanc.
key_facts: 17 commercial vineyards on about 1,000 acres, and 6 wineries (T.D. TTB-155)
The Van Duzer Corridor is Oregon's lowest pass through the Coast Range

sources.title: 27 CFR 9.265, Van Duzer Corridor (eCFR text via Cornell LII)
Federal Register final rule (govinfo), T.D. TTB-155, Van Duzer Corridor (2018)
Willamette Valley Wineries Association, Van Duzer Corridor AVA overview
Willamette Valley Wineries Association, McMinnville AVA overview

article.description: An AVA of about 59,000 acres around the hamlets of Carlton and Yamhill in Yamhill and Washington counties, entirely within the Willamette Valley AVA, limited by law to land between 200 and 1,000 feet. Low ridges ring the two towns in a horseshoe, with the North Yamhill River running through. It was named Yamhill-Carlton District until 2010.
article.climate: Sheltered on three sides: the Coast Range to the west, nearly 3,500 feet high, casts a rain shadow, and the Chehalem Mountains to the north and the Dundee Hills to the east add further protection.
article.soils: Coarse-grained ancient marine sediments, among the oldest soils in the valley, which drain quickly and leave the vines short of water.
article.grape_varieties: Pinot Noir makes up about 80% of plantings, with Chardonnay and Pinot Gris.
article.wine_styles: Mostly red wine from Pinot Noir, with white wines from Chardonnay and Pinot Gris.
key_facts: Limited to land between 200 and 1,000 feet (27 CFR 9.183)
About 2,844 acres planted in 127 vineyards (Willamette Valley Wineries Association)

sources.title: 27 CFR 9.183, Yamhill-Carlton (eCFR text via Cornell LII)
Willamette Valley Wineries Association, Yamhill-Carlton AVA overview

article.description: An AVA of 162,762 acres in central Washington around the town of Quincy, in Douglas, Grant and Kittitas counties, with the Columbia River along its western edge. It is named for the lakes that dot its ice-age flood channels. It is one of the few Washington AVAs planted more to white grapes than to red, above all Riesling.
article.climate: One of the more northerly parts of the Columbia Valley, with many vineyards a little higher than the valley around them, so heat builds later in the season and fades sooner. Wide swings between day and night help the grapes keep their acidity, and the Columbia River shields many sites from early and late frost.
article.soils: Soils left by the Missoula Floods, mostly fine sand with silt and sandy loam; some sites, such as Evergreen Vineyard, have deposits of calcium-rich caliche. Most of the area slopes gently, at under 4%, toward its eastern boundary.
article.grape_varieties: Riesling leads the plantings, with Chardonnay and Sauvignon Blanc among the more than 20 varieties grown.
article.wine_styles: Mostly white wines, led by Riesling, Chardonnay and Sauvignon Blanc, with some red wines.
key_facts: About 162,762 acres, with six commercial vineyards on about 1,399 acres at approval (T.D. TTB-108)
Part of the Channeled Scablands, carved by the ice-age floods

sources.title: 27 CFR 9.227, Ancient Lakes of Columbia Valley (eCFR text via Cornell LII)
Federal Register final rule (govinfo), T.D. TTB-108, Ancient Lakes of Columbia Valley (2012)
Washington State Wine Commission, AVA profile: Ancient Lakes of Columbia Valley
Great Northwest Wine (HeraldNet), Ancient Lakes fascinates as young Washington wine region (2017)

article.description: A large AVA in south-central Washington, in Benton, Klickitat and Yakima counties, rising north from the Columbia River. Its name comes from an early pioneer who, seeing its wide prairies, called it horse heaven. About a quarter of Washington's wine-grape acreage is planted here, much of it on south-facing slopes.
article.climate: Warm and windy, with an arid to semi-arid continental climate, so vineyards are irrigated. Steady winds keep canopies small and grape skins thick and discourage mold and rot, and the Columbia River tempers the risk of early and late frost.
article.soils: Three main soil types, all well drained: wind-blown sand and loess, Missoula Flood sediment, and rubble washed down the hill slopes from the Columbia River basalt bedrock.
article.grape_varieties: Cabernet Sauvignon makes up a large share of plantings, with Merlot, Chardonnay and Riesling.
article.wine_styles: Red wines led by Cabernet Sauvignon and Merlot, and white wines from Chardonnay and Riesling.
key_facts: About 570,000 acres, about 17,082 under vine (Washington State Wine Commission)
First vinifera planted in 1972, at what is now Champoux Vineyard

sources.title: 27 CFR 9.188, Horse Heaven Hills (eCFR text via Cornell LII)
Washington State Wine Commission, AVA profile: Horse Heaven Hills

article.description: An AVA of about 24,040 acres wrapped around the southern end of Lake Chelan in north-central Washington, in Chelan County, within the Columbia Valley AVA. Unlike most of the Columbia Valley it sits on granitic rather than basalt bedrock, and it lies north of the reach of the Missoula Floods. Its first modern vinifera plantings date from 1998.
article.climate: The glacier-carved lake, up to 1,486 feet deep, moderates the climate: summer days are cooler and summer nights warmer than in the land around it. Vineyards lie along the southern and eastern shores at about 1,100 feet, higher than many southern parts of the Columbia Valley.
article.soils: Glacial sediments with a good deal of quartz and mica, mixed with ash and pumice from the volcanoes of the Cascade Range.
article.grape_varieties: Syrah and Pinot Noir lead, with Chardonnay, Pinot Gris, Merlot and Riesling.
article.wine_styles: Red wines from Syrah, Pinot Noir and Merlot, and white wines from Chardonnay, Pinot Gris and Riesling.
key_facts: About 24,040 acres, about 269 under vine (Washington State Wine Commission)
Parts of its boundary follow the 2,000-foot elevation line (27 CFR 9.215)

sources.title: 27 CFR 9.215, Lake Chelan (eCFR text via Cornell LII)
Washington State Wine Commission, AVA profile: Lake Chelan

article.description: An AVA of about 13,254 acres on a plateau northwest of Yakima, between the towns of Naches and Tieton in Yakima County, within the Columbia Valley AVA. It sits on a lava flow about a million years old with andesite bedrock, rather than the basalt found across most of the Columbia Valley. Its first vinifera were planted in 2002.
article.climate: At 1,200 to 2,100 feet and close to the Cascades, it is cooler and wetter than much of the Columbia Valley, with 10 to 13 inches of rain a year. The plateau's gentle grade lets cold air drain to lower ground, lowering the risk of frost.
article.soils: Wholly above the level of the Missoula Floods, so the soils are wind-blown loess, still accumulating, with a good deal of clay that helps hold water.
article.grape_varieties: Pinot Gris and Riesling lead, with Gewürztraminer and Syrah.
article.wine_styles: Mostly white wines from Pinot Gris, Riesling and Gewürztraminer, and red wine from Syrah.
key_facts: Every vineyard is farmed organically, biodynamically or Salmon-Safe, or a mix of these

sources.title: 27 CFR 9.222, Naches Heights (eCFR text via Cornell LII)
Washington State Wine Commission, AVA profile: Naches Heights

article.description: An AVA of about 32,333 acres straddling the Columbia River between Wenatchee and Lake Chelan, in Chelan and Douglas counties, within the Columbia Valley AVA. The river and the Rocky Reach Reservoir cover about a quarter of it. Its name comes from steamboat captains of the late 1800s, who used it for this rocky stretch of rapids.
article.climate: The low terraces in the river canyon are warmer, with a longer growing season, than the mountains and plateaus around them, which lets grapes ripen this far north. About 11 inches of rain falls a year.
article.soils: Wind-blown sand and silt over cobblestones and gravel left by glacial outwash and floods, on crystalline bedrock rich in quartz and mica, which among Columbia Valley AVAs it shares only with Lake Chelan. The stony surface warms quickly and gives off heat to the vines.
article.grape_varieties: Cabernet Sauvignon is the leading grape on its roughly 117 acres of vineyards.
article.wine_styles: Mainly red wines, led by Cabernet Sauvignon.
key_facts: 7 commercial vineyards on about 117 acres at approval (T.D. TTB-183)
About 24% of the area is river and reservoir

article.description: An AVA of about 156,389 acres in Grant and Adams counties: a broad, mostly south-facing slope around Royal City between the Quincy Basin and the Saddle Mountains, within the Columbia Valley AVA. It lies between the Ancient Lakes AVA to the north and the Wahluke Slope to the south. Wine grapes were first planted here in 1983.
article.climate: Cooler than the Wahluke Slope about 15 miles south and warmer than Ancient Lakes, with 6 to 8 inches of rain a year. Elevations run from 610 feet to 1,756 feet on the Frenchman Hills ridge; higher sites ripen later and keep more acidity, and the slope lets cold air drain away.
article.soils: Fine sand with silt and sandy loam, on a slope that is part of the Yakima Fold Belt.
article.grape_varieties: Cabernet Sauvignon leads, with Syrah and Chardonnay among a wide range of varieties.
article.wine_styles: Red wines led by Cabernet Sauvignon and Syrah, and white wines such as Chardonnay.
key_facts: 13 commercial vineyards and one winery (Washington State Wine Commission)
Much of its boundary follows the 250-meter elevation contour (27 CFR 9.271)

article.description: An AVA of about 16,870 acres in Klickitat County, on benches above the Columbia River west of the Horse Heaven Hills, within the Columbia Valley AVA. The name has been used for the area for more than 100 years, though its origin is unclear. Almost all of its vineyards have been planted since 2015.
article.climate: It averages about 2,763 growing degree days, a little above the Columbia Valley's norm, but steady winds from the nearby Columbia Gorge slow the vines and keep canopies and berries small, so harvest comes late. It averages 8.76 inches of rain a year, more than much of the valley.
article.soils: Mainly silty loams of the Mollisol order, largely Walla Walla silt loam, which hold more water and organic matter than the soils around them, on southeast-facing benches with an average slope of about 7%.
article.grape_varieties: Cabernet Sauvignon is the main grape, and Syrah the other most planted variety.
article.wine_styles: Red wines, chiefly from Cabernet Sauvignon and Syrah.
key_facts: 3 commercial vineyards on about 1,261 acres at approval (T.D. TTB-168)
Precipitation of about 6.7 to 10.4 inches a year across the area (T.D. TTB-168)

article.description: An AVA of about 81,000 acres near Mattawa in Grant County, bounded by the Columbia River, the Saddle Mountains and the Hanford Reach National Monument, within the Columbia Valley AVA. The whole AVA sits on one large ancestral alluvial fan with a steady grade of under 8%. It holds about 15% of Washington's vineyard acreage.
article.climate: Among the warmest and driest parts of the state, with about 6 inches of rain a year. The slope and the nearby Columbia River lower the risk of frost; elevations run from 425 feet at the river to 1,480 feet, though most vineyards lie below 1,000 feet.
article.soils: Deep wind-blown sand, more than 5 feet deep on average, which drains freely and makes vine vigor and ripening unusually even across the area.
article.grape_varieties: Mainly red grapes, above all Cabernet Sauvignon, Merlot and Syrah, with Chardonnay.
article.wine_styles: Red wines from Cabernet Sauvignon, Merlot and Syrah, and some white wine from Chardonnay.
key_facts: About 8,932 acres under vine (Washington State Wine Commission)
Its name is a Native American term for 'watering place'

article.description: An AVA of about 300,000 acres around the town of Walla Walla that spans Walla Walla County, Washington, and Umatilla County, Oregon; TTB lists both states. It lies within the Columbia Valley AVA and holds The Rocks District of Milton-Freewater, on the Oregon side. It has the highest concentration of wineries in Washington, including some of the state's oldest.
article.climate: Cooler and wetter than many Washington AVAs. Rainfall rises from about 9 inches a year in the west to 22 inches at the eastern edge in the foothills of the Blue Mountains, where a few vineyards can be farmed without irrigation.
article.soils: Mostly well-drained sandy loess over Missoula Flood slackwater deposits and fractured basalt; above 1,200 feet, the floods' high-water mark, the loess lies directly on basalt. In the south an old riverbed of cobblestones defines The Rocks District.
article.grape_varieties: Mostly red grapes, led by Cabernet Sauvignon, Merlot and Syrah.
article.wine_styles: Mainly red wines from Cabernet Sauvignon, Merlot and Syrah.
key_facts: About 2,933 acres under vine, 1,672 of them in Washington (Washington State Wine Commission)
More than 120 wineries (Washington State Wine Commission)
Its name comes from a Native American term meaning 'many waters'

article.description: An AVA of about 93,738 acres in Franklin County, on a plateau north of Pasco that rises about 200 feet above the land around it, within the Columbia Valley AVA. It is named for the whitish lake-bed sediments of the Ringold Formation, exposed in bluffs along the Columbia River. Its first vines were planted in 1972.
article.climate: The plateau's height lengthens the growing season by about 45 days on average compared with the surrounding area and helps protect vines from frost and freezes. About 6 inches of rain falls a year.
article.soils: Wind-deposited silt and fine sand over ice-age flood sediment, on the clay-rich lake-bed sediments of the Ringold Formation and a thick layer of caliche, so vine roots never reach basalt.
article.grape_varieties: Cabernet Sauvignon and Merlot lead, with Syrah, Riesling and Sauvignon Blanc.
article.wine_styles: Red wines from Cabernet Sauvignon, Merlot and Syrah, and white wines from Riesling and Sauvignon Blanc.
key_facts: 9 commercial vineyards on about 1,127 acres, and one winery (T.D. TTB-167)
Elevations of about 700 to 1,200 feet (T.D. TTB-167)

article.description: Washington's first AVA, established in 1983 in Benton and Yakima counties within the Columbia Valley AVA, and the first in the Pacific Northwest. The Yakima River runs through it, and it holds nearly a third of the state's planted vinifera acreage. It contains the Red Mountain, Rattlesnake Hills, Snipes Mountain, Goose Gap and Candy Mountain AVAs.
article.climate: Cooler toward the Cascade foothills in the west and hot toward the center of the Columbia Basin, with about 8 inches of rain a year; the Yakima River and local aquifers supply water for irrigation.
article.soils: Moderate to deep silt loam laid down by the Missoula Floods, over gravel or directly on basalt bedrock, well drained for irrigated vines.
article.grape_varieties: One of the few Washington AVAs planted more to white grapes than red, led by Chardonnay and Riesling; its warmer sites grow Merlot, Cabernet Sauvignon and Syrah.
article.wine_styles: White wines from Chardonnay and Riesling, and red wines from Merlot, Cabernet Sauvignon and Syrah.
key_facts: About 18,924 acres under vine (Washington State Wine Commission)
Boundary extended by about 72 acres in 2020 to take in Candy Mountain (T.D. TTB-163)

article.description: An AVA of about 815 acres on the southwest-facing slope of Candy Mountain in Benton County, four miles southeast of Red Mountain. It lies within the Yakima Valley and Columbia Valley AVAs: T.D. TTB-163 extended Yakima Valley by about 72 acres to take it in whole. It is one of Washington's smallest AVAs.
article.climate: Warm and dry, with about 5 inches of rain a year, and windier than the land around it, much like Red Mountain nearby.
article.soils: Thin soils of wind-deposited silt and fine sand over ice-age flood sediment and basalt bedrock; they hold little water, so growers can stress the vines as they choose.
article.grape_varieties: Cabernet Sauvignon is the leading grape.
article.wine_styles: Red wines, mainly from Cabernet Sauvignon.
key_facts: Elevations of 640 to 1,320 feet, on slopes of 2 to 20 degrees (T.D. TTB-163)
About 110 acres under vine (Washington State Wine Commission)

article.description: An AVA of about 8,129 acres in Benton County, taking in Goose Mountain and the gap between it and Badger and Candy mountains, within the Yakima Valley and Columbia Valley AVAs. Goose Mountain's ridge runs east to west, unlike the northwest-trending ridges of Red Mountain, Candy Mountain and Rattlesnake Mountain, so most vines face north-northeast. The gap is named for the migratory waterfowl that pass through it.
article.climate: On north-facing slopes the grapes receive less sun than on the south- and southwest-facing sites nearby and usually ripen later than the same varieties on Red Mountain. About 6 inches of rain falls a year.
article.soils: Almost two thirds Warden series soils, wind-blown silt and fine sand over Missoula Flood sediment, with Kiona, Shano, Hezel and Prosser series; elevations run from 577 to 1,339 feet.
article.grape_varieties: Cabernet Sauvignon leads, with Merlot, Syrah and Chardonnay among the 16 varieties planted.
article.wine_styles: Red wines led by Cabernet Sauvignon, Merlot and Syrah, and white wine from Chardonnay.
key_facts: Two vineyards on more than 1,800 acres, and one winery (T.D. TTB-170)
First vines planted in 1998 by Arvid Monson

article.description: An AVA of about 68,500 acres on the south slope of the Rattlesnake Hills around Zillah in Yakima County, within the Yakima Valley AVA. The hills are an east-west fold of the Yakima Fold Belt and take their name from nearby Rattlesnake Mountain. The earliest vines here were planted in 1968.
article.climate: Generally higher than the Yakima Valley as a whole, from 850 to 3,085 feet, with vineyards on the lower ground; the height lessens the risk of spring and fall frost, and winters are milder than in the land around it. Rainfall is 6 to 12 inches a year.
article.soils: Mostly silt loam and loam. About half the AVA is underlain by Ellensburg Formation sediments eroded from the Cascade volcanoes, and the higher vineyards lie above the reach of the Missoula Floods.
article.grape_varieties: Fairly evenly split between red and white grapes, reds slightly ahead: Merlot, Cabernet Sauvignon, Syrah and Riesling lead.
article.wine_styles: Red wines from Merlot, Cabernet Sauvignon and Syrah, and white wine from Riesling.
key_facts: About 1,807 acres under vine (Washington State Wine Commission)
Its boundary crosses Elephant Mountain, Zillah Peak and High Top Mountain (27 CFR 9.193)

article.description: An AVA of about 4,040 acres near Benton City in Benton County, within the Yakima Valley AVA. Despite its name it is neither red nor a mountain but a fold of the Yakima Fold Belt with broad southwest-facing slopes; in spring its cheatgrass turns a reddish hue. Cabernet Sauvignon makes up about 60% of its plantings.
article.climate: One of Washington's warmest and driest AVAs, with about 5 inches of rain a year. The nearby Yakima River keeps the air moving and guards against frost, and nights can be as much as 40 °F cooler than days.
article.soils: Sandy loam and gravel, alkaline and rich in calcium carbonate; the lean, high-pH soils limit vine vigor and keep berries small.
article.grape_varieties: Cabernet Sauvignon dominates, with Merlot and Syrah.
article.wine_styles: Red wines, mainly Cabernet Sauvignon, Merlot and Syrah, often firmly tannic.
key_facts: About 2,382 acres under vine (Washington State Wine Commission)
More than 15 wineries (Washington State Wine Commission)

article.description: An AVA of about 4,145 acres on Snipes Mountain, a fold of the Yakima Fold Belt between Sunnyside and Granger in Yakima County, within the Yakima Valley AVA. It is named after cattle rancher Ben Snipes, who built a home at its base in the 1800s. Vineyards were first planted here in 1914, and Harrison Hill holds Cabernet Sauvignon vines from 1963.
article.climate: Steep north- and south-facing slopes let cold air drain downhill, helping to prevent the frost damage that sometimes hits nearby areas. About 7 inches of rain falls a year.
article.soils: Loess over Missoula Flood sediment and, in many places, fist- to melon-sized cobbles and gravel laid down by an ancestral course of the Columbia River; only the top 90 feet of the mountain rise above the floods.
article.grape_varieties: Chardonnay, Cabernet Sauvignon and Merlot lead the plantings.
article.wine_styles: Red wines from Cabernet Sauvignon and Merlot, and white wine from Chardonnay.
key_facts: About 859 acres under vine (Washington State Wine Commission)
Its boundary follows the 750-foot and 820-foot elevation contours (27 CFR 9.213)
